questions.question: A configuration file contains max_speed = fast. What should the parser do?
options: Return either the setting or the reason there is none, in a form the caller cannot ignore
Return a sensible default and carry on
Print a message and call exit
Throw, so the problem cannot be missed
questions.explanation: A default means the robot runs at a speed nobody chose. Exiting takes the machine down for a typo. Returning the failure lets the caller decide with full context.

questions.question: Which kind of failure should be handled with an assertion rather than a return value?
options: A bug, such as indexing past the end of an array
A file that is missing
A serial port that is busy
Input that does not parse
questions.explanation: A bug is not to be handled, it is to be fixed, so it should fail loudly in testing. The other three are expected failures that a correct program meets in normal operation.

questions.question: When is std::optional the right return type rather than expected?
options: When something may simply be absent and the reason adds nothing
Whenever the function can fail
Only when the value is a number
When the caller is going to ignore the result
questions.explanation: Looking up a setting that was never configured has one obvious reason. Parsing has five, and an operator needs to know which, so that one returns expected.

questions.question: Why does the reference check both in.fail() and in.eof() after reading a number?
options: Without the eof check, 1.5kg parses as 1.5 and the rest is silently discarded
Because eof is set before fail
To detect an empty string
Because streams throw on failure otherwise
questions.explanation: The failure check catches text that is not a number at all. The end of input check catches text that begins with one and continues.

questions.question: Why do many robotics and embedded codebases build with exceptions disabled?
options: Throwing allocates and unwinds with no stateable bound, which a loop with a deadline cannot accept
Because exceptions are slower in every case
Because C++ exceptions do not work on ARM
Because error codes are easier to read
questions.explanation: The objection is the unbounded worst case rather than the average cost. Some safety standards effectively require it, and a returned error is also handled where the context still exists.

questions.question: What remains a good use of throwing, even in this style?
options: A constructor that cannot produce a valid object
A file that does not exist
A value that fails validation
A device that is already in use
questions.explanation: A constructor has no return value, so throwing is the only way to refuse to create an object that would break its own invariants. The other three are ordinary outcomes.
